Lessons.Title: Estimate and Measure Liquid Volume
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade 3 Unit 6 Lesson 8 under CCSS 3.MD.A.2 is about estimating container capacity and interpreting graduated liter marks. Source teacher lesson.html SHA256 3d06f08e6406434fb7dbf8ed00e4cffe810c38c055c386b47e1841572fc1f9c9 and preparation.html SHA256 4e697c77131e157b50a759c568664242ea60cb23911020341a95fc7d8b61170f were reviewed from the owner's local Common Core archive. Three student-facing sections and source image descriptions are available locally. The independent PDF and original image pixels were NOT inspected; no numerical answer is invented for original diagram A–H.

Warm-up Number Talk Divide by 3 (10 min): EXACT four original calculations30÷3=10,60÷3=20,63÷3=21,54÷3=18. Teacher encourages mentally doubling 30÷3 and adding one group of3 to the result of60÷3; more than one correct student strategy may be accepted. These scalar results are exact mathematical checks.

Activity1 Estimate Liquid Volume (15 min) starts with ORIGINAL three pupils' bathtub estimates: Clare about2 liters, Jada about20 liters, Kiran about200 liters. The source teacher gives Kiran as the reasonable model estimate for the pictured large bathtub, not a physical measurement of the photographed vessel. Pupils choose which guess is plausible and justify it with earlier 1-liter experiences. The same original choices2L,20L,200L are used to discuss a BOTTLE and BUCKET; a small bottle may be around2L, a bucket around20L, not200L. These are reasoned approximations, not guaranteed product capacities.

Activity1 then shows EXACT four pictured categories: SINK, KIDDIE POOL, POT and TOILET TANK, with EXACT four source cards 4L,6L,500L,10L. A plausible one-to-one estimate is pot4L, toilet tank6L, sink10L and kiddie pool500L. Teacher checks reasoning because actual physical container capacities vary with design/size. This is a contextual ESTIMATION task; not a measured manufacturer-spec identification.

Activity2 Measure Liquid Volume (20 min) compares marked graduated containers and rulers, requiring careful attention to ZERO at bottom and different tick increments. Source asks 'What do you notice? What do you wonder?' about the visual markings and then 'The container in each image is marked in liters. Find the volume of the liquid' for EIGHT original figures labelled A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H. Each original liquid level is a visually encoded numerical quantity. These eight figure images are NOT inspected at source-pixel level in the local archive; no numeric values for A-H are certified or silently invented. Original teacher must check their actual physical tick locations and labels. Maintain all eight separate pupil tasks with a TEACHER_VISUAL_REVIEW gate.

Activity2 secondly asks pupils to SHADE five originally EMPTY liter containers to the prescribed levels: P:1 liter;Q:8 liters;R:7 liters;S:2 1/2 liters;T:23 liters. Preserve all five original labels and values, not just a generic fill-in question. The source's bottle/scale drawings differ in vertical range and marked intervals; teacher must verify selected shade height relative to actual scale, even when the intended numeric volume is known.

Optional question from original Activity2: from ALL containers in the activity, decide which TWO have the most liquid and add their volumes. The answer depends on the actual recorded A-H source-diagram readings and whether completed P-T volumes are included under the teacher's task interpretation. Do not hardcode 'T plus Q=31 liters' without confirming source illustrated A-H values and interpretation; ask teacher to review the two numerically largest actually shown after all drawings are resolved.

Source teacher advancing-thinking text distinguishes intervals: a midpoint between2L and4L is3L, and between4L and6L is5L (the marks for container D). On container F, four equally spaced marks strictly between10L and15L can represent11L,12L,13L,14L; each subdivision is1 liter. These are SOURCE INFERENCES about scale subdivision, not the unknown pictured final water level. Between3L and4L the half-mark is3 1/2L. Teacher helps students name intervals before reading or drawing liquid levels.

Student section summary returns to prior reference weights: paper clip about1 gram, basket of apples about1 kilogram, and introduces a container calibrated in liters. Original independently downloaded student PDF, source photo pixel values, publisher teacher-gated Cool-down Measure in Liters, tests, Stage D, academic approval and production rendering remain unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate liquid capacity
KeyConcepts.Definition: A reasoned liter estimate identifies a plausible magnitude, not an exact certified physical capacity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Choose plausible unit count for object size and justify.
KeyConcepts.Example: Source Kiran estimates a bathtub about200L rather than2L or20L.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graduated liquid container
KeyConcepts.Definition: Graduations represent accumulated volume measured upward from zero when standing level.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check numbered marks, count equal intervals, read actual liquid surface.
KeyConcepts.Example: From10L to15L with four interior marks, step size is1L.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mark a target volume
KeyConcepts.Definition: To shade a labeled container, place liquid level at the corresponding volume on that container's own scale.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The same liters can have different picture heights depending on vessel geometry and scale.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate vs source exact diagram
KeyConcepts.Definition: Original visual figures A-H require checking the actual published image before asserting an exact reading.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Never assign fixed numbers from short alt-text captions alone.
KeyConcepts.Example: A-H remain teacher visual-review tasks; only scale-subdivision guidance is source-confirmed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original four division facts
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute30÷3,60÷3,63÷3,54÷3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use known multiplication facts, doubling and add/subtract thirds.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original bathtub estimates
WorkedExamples.Question: Which of Clare2L, Jada20L and Kiran200L is a plausible pictured bathtub capacity?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare size of bathtub to remembered 1-liter amount.
Steps: 2 liters is far too small for a full bathtub.
20 liters remains small for a full bathtub.
200 liters is a plausible capacity estimate for the pictured category.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Kiran about200 liters as a reasonable estimate
WorkedExamples.Check: Not an exact measured volume of original photograph.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four physical categories, original choice cards
WorkedExamples.Question: Make plausible matches for sink, kiddie pool, pot and toilet tank to 4L,6L,500L,10L.
WorkedExamples.Check: Student must justify, actual products vary.

WorkedExamples.Title: Teacher source interval reading
WorkedExamples.Question: Between 10 and15 liters are four equally spaced interior tick marks. What do they represent?
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not confuse this scale inference with container F's actual unknown waterline.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source five shade requests
WorkedExamples.Question: How much should containers P,Q,R,S,T be shaded?
WorkedExamples.Method: Follow each originally printed target mark on its own scale.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks each final shaded image.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Force exact numeric capacity for pictured bathtub/bottle/bucket.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original task is estimating likely capacity, not reading measured manufactured specifications.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State plausibility with context and reason.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original cards are different orders of magnitude.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare to benchmark1L and real vessel sizes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Invent readings for A-H from image names or chapter topic.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Water heights and scale ticks not preserved as numeric text in locally reviewed source.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep all eight under original figure/teacher review before accepting readings.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Shade every P-T vessel by identical picture height for same number of liters.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Vessel drawing scale and spacing can differ.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use graduations on each pictured vessel.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume four internal ticks from10 to15 each represent one fourth liter.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The interval spans5L across five equal gaps.

SummaryPoints: Bathtub original estimates2,20,200 liters (Clare/Jada/Kiran); Kiran200L plausibly best, not physically certified.
